newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Kohl calls for calm as tempers flare on tax.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl calls for calm as tempers flare on tax.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Monday had to tell some of his most senior government members to stop bickering in public as an embarassing rift on possible tax increases within his coalition refused to heal.

His appeal came after Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt engaged in a slanging match after Waigel had accused other government departments of ruining his budget sums with botched economic forecasts.

Kohl, himself taking no position on whether Germany would need to raise taxes to ensure it meets Maastricht criteria for European economic and monetary union, said calm discussion rather than public rowing was in order.
"Let's talk to each other first before we start talking about each other," Kohl told journalists at a meeting of executives of his Christian Democrats (CDU) in Bonn.
He said the 1998 budget and the question of whether there was a need for a mini-budget this year would all be on the agenda of formal budget discussions due on July 2.
Waigel has refused to rule out tax increases to help him cut borrowing this year to meet the strict budget deficit limit required to qualify for EMU.

On Sunday he drew a stinging rebuke from his cabinet colleague Rexrodt, a member of the Free Democrat (FDP) junior coalition partners, after blaming other government departments of hindering his attempts to get public finances in order.

Rexrodt abandoned all show of ministerial solidarity to condemn Waigel's comments, contained in an interview with the weekly 'Der Spiegel' magazine, as a "transparent manoeuvre to distract from his own faults".

Government heayweights on Monday leapt to defend Waigel, with CDU general secretary Peter Hintze accusing the free-market FDP of losing all touch with reality by insisting that Waigel rule out tax rises to help the budget.

"You cannot simply substitute oaths for the rules of mathematics," Hintze said on German radio, referring to the FDP's newly-agreed party resolution ruling out any rise in taxes to plug budget shortfalls.

The FDP, at a weekend party conference, adopted a motion opposing tax increases and insisting the Kohl coalition sticks to a deal to cut the solidarity surcharge -- a tax raised to help pay for German unification -- by two points next year.

But Hintze said the FDP's insistence on fiscal rigidity, coupled with their desire to continue investment in the recession-hit east of the country, would provide Germany with yet more budget problems.

"When the FDP say they want to increase investments in the east, when they say they want to reduce the solidarity tax (funding east German development) and when they say no to new borrowing, you have a mathematical dilemma that's pretty hard to solve," Hintze said.

Kohl's Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said the FDP must simply recognise that nothing could be ruled out in Germany's race to square its budgets, made even more pressing ahead of the single European currency.
"It's no use putting handcuffs on yourself...We must sit together and nothing must be left out of the discussion," Bohl said on radio.
